tip: In a guess the tense lives on 같다 (gatda = seem): 긴장한 것 같았어요 (ginjanghan geot gatasseoyo) = it seemed he was nervous – 같았어요 is past because the seeming was then.
말씀 (malsseum) = honored 'words/speech' of an elder.
행복하시길 바라요 (haengbokhasigil barayo): the -시- inside honors the couple being wished well, while plain 바라요 (barayo = I hope) is your own act – no honoring yourself.
Verbs sit in front of nouns like adjectives: 좋아하는 가수 (joahaneun gasu) = 'the liking singer', i.e. the singer I like. English puts the clause after; Korean packs it before, with -는.
만에 after a time span = 'in only that long': 십 분 만에 (sip bun mane) = in just ten minutes. It carries the surprise at the speed – the tickets vanished that fast.
-자마자 means 'as soon as' with zero gap: 나오자마자 (naojamaja) = the instant it came out. The two actions touch – no time allowed between release and purchase.
'And' between nouns picks its shape by sound: 와 (wa) after vowels, 과 (gwa) after consonants. 춤 (chum) ends in a consonant, so it's 춤과 노래 (chumgwa norae) = dance and song.
세 곡이나 (se gogina) isn't just 'three songs' – the -이나 adds surprise at the amount: 'three whole songs!'. Drop it and the number turns neutral.
여운이 남았어요 (yeouni namasseoyo): 여운 is literally the lingering sound after a note ends, and 남다 (namda) = remain. Korean says the concert's echo stayed behind.
-부터 (buteo) marks the starting point: 데뷔 때부터 (debwi ttaebuteo) = from the time of their debut. 때 (ttae = time) plus -부터 builds 'ever since' for any event.
Reported 'let's' has its own ending: -자고 하다. 가자고 했어요 (gajago haesseoyo) = said 'let's go' – the 자 (ja) carries the suggestion, so no quotation marks needed.
Korean location words are nouns: 무대 위 (mudae wi) = 'the stage's top'. With -의 (e) it modifies the next noun: 무대 위의 가수 (mudae wie gasu) = the on-stage singer.
방 (bang = room) builds venues: 노래방 (noraebang) = song-room, i.e. karaoke. The same pattern gives PC방 (PC-bang, internet cafe) and 찜질방 (jjimjilbang, sauna).
를 위해 (reul wihae) = 'for the sake of': 가수를 위해 (gasureul wihae) = for their singer. It marks who benefits – stronger and more deliberate than plain 'for'.
Purpose of movement gets its own ending: 보러 갔어요 (boreo gasseoyo) = went in order to watch. -(으)러 normally attaches to going and coming verbs – it states why you moved.
바탕 (batang) = base or foundation: 실화를 바탕으로 (silhwareul batangeuro) = 'with a true story as the base'. That's how Korean says 'based on' – the source is the ground under it.
You don't 'be popular' in Korean – you have lots of popularity: 인기가 많아요 (ingiga manayo), literally 'popularity is plentiful'. Popularity is a possession, not a trait.
사서 먹었어요 (saseo meogeosseoyo) = bought it and ate that very popcorn – -아/어서 keeps the first action's result in hand. Plain -고 would just list two separate acts.
몰다 (molda) = to herd or drive together: 몰아서 봤어요 (moraseo bwasseoyo) = watched them herded into one sitting. Korean binge-watching literally rounds the episodes up.
-적인 turns idea-nouns into adjectives: 감동 (gamdong = deep emotion) grows into 감동적인 (gamdongjeogin) = moving. One suffix, hundreds of instant adjectives.
-기 전에 (-gi jeone) = 'before': 시작하기 전에 (sijakhagi jeone) = before it starts.
없이 (eopsi) after a noun = 'without it': 자막 없이 (jamak eopsi) = without subtitles. It's the adverb form of 없다 (eopda = to not exist) – 'the subtitles not existing'.
원작 (wonjak) = the original work: 소설을 원작으로 해요 (soseoreul wonjageuro haeyo) = takes the novel as its original. This is the set pattern for calling something an adaptation.
-고도 = 'even after / even just': 예고편만 보고도 (yegopyeonman bogodo) = even just from watching the trailer. It flags a result arriving earlier than expected – tears before the film.
'Must not' is built from 'if': 찍으면 안 돼요 (jjigeumyeon an dwaeyo) is literally 'if you photograph, it won't do'. Korean often bans things by condition rather than command.
-아/어야 means 'only if': 예약을 해야 볼 수 있어요 (yeyageul haeya bol su isseoyo) = only if you reserve can you see it. The condition ending itself carries the 'only'.
An elder subject takes the honorific present: 좋아하세요 (joahaseyo) = she likes it.
Hours of duration use native numbers: 세 시간 (se sigan) = three hours.
Chaining 주다 (juda = give) after a verb turns it into a favor for someone: 보여 주세요 (boyeo juseyo) = show it – for me. Korean marks who benefits right inside the verb.
(으)로 marks the choice: 창가 자리로 (changga jariro) = as a window seat.
